posts.title: Why Every Bulb We Sell Is 2700K
posts.excerpt: A calm look at colour temperature, domestic evening rituals, and why warm 2700K illumination is the quiet foundation of every lamp at Steenkade 14.
posts.content:
When Ines Varga founded Hikari Lighting at Steenkade 14 in Rotterdam in 2016, she made a deliberate technical decision: every lamp leaving our workshop would ship fitted with a 2700K warm white bulb. That decision has remained unchanged through ten years of showroom life and residential projects. In modern lighting retail, consumers are constantly offered endless colour temperature options, adjustable RGB chips, and cool white daylight arrays. Yet when dusk settles across the stone quays of Rotterdam, the human eye does not crave artificial daylight. It seeks warmth, depth, and rest.

The colour temperature scale measures the spectral warmth of light in kelvins. High numbers, such as 4000K or 5000K, produce a crisp, blue-tinted radiance reminiscent of high noon on an overcast day. Such temperatures have their place in commercial laboratories, assembly lines, and surgery rooms where visual alertness is paramount. However, when brought into a living room or a small dining room, cool light flattens the environment. It leaches richness from natural materials, exposes harsh edges, and tells the human body that daytime tasks must continue. At 2700K, the spectrum shifts decisively toward warm amber, mirroring the gentle emission of traditional carbon filament lamps, candles, and evening fires.

This warm spectral quality is essential because of how light interacts with honest interior finishes. In our showroom bays at Steenkade 14, we test fixtures against honed limestone, dark lime plaster, solid oak, and natural linen. Under a 2700K bulb, an unbleached linen drum shade like the one on our Bay Floor Lamp filters light into a soft golden pool. A turned oak body or a stoneware base, like that on the Cairn Table Lamp, reveals its tactile grain and quiet imperfections. When you suspend a fixture such as the Low Pendant Trio over an oak dining table, the 2700K warmth illuminates the table surface without spilling glare into diners' eyes.

Restraint is the heart of good illumination. Light should be the quietest furniture in the room, guiding attention rather than demanding it. In our home consultations across Rotterdam, lighting planner Tomasz Rehn frequently encounters rooms compromised by excessive overhead illumination. A single ceiling luminaire running at 3000K or 4000K casts unforgiving downward shadows, making spaces feel clinical and restless. By committing to 2700K across all six pieces on our monthly floor, we encourage clients to layer their illumination. A floor lamp anchors a low seating corner, a table lamp warms a bookshelf, and a wall fixture guides a hallway. Each pool of light remains calm, soft, and localized.

Every lamp we sell at Hikari Lighting includes an E27 2700K bulb tested for smooth performance with trailing-edge dimmers. Dimming a 2700K source lowers intensity while preserving its soothing evening quality, allowing a room to transition gracefully from dinner preparation to late-night reading. To see this in practice, visitors can experience our six floor pieces on low stone plinths during open hours, or take advantage of our seven-day home trial for a fifty-euro refundable deposit. Testing a lamp on your own walls after dark is the only true way to understand how 2700K light settles into a home.

posts.title: Rewiring a 1960s brass lamp
posts.excerpt: A look inside our workshop bench as Sam Okoro restores original brass switchgear, replaces perished braided cord, and fits modern ceramic E27 sockets.
posts.content:
A lamp from the 1960s usually arrives with brittle cloth cord and a socket that no longer holds a bulb straight. Sam Okoro strips it to the brass, tests every part and keeps what can be kept.

The new cord is braided cotton, the socket is ceramic E27, and the lamp leaves the bench with a safety test. Rewiring and repair starts from €65.

posts.title: How a linen shade is made
posts.excerpt: Shade maker Lucía Ferraz demonstrates the careful process of patterning, tensioning, and hand-stretching unbleached linen over solid wire drum frames.
posts.content:
Lucía Ferraz starts with a paper pattern cut to the frame, then stretches unbleached linen over a wire drum, pinning it while it is still slack.

The seam is glued, the edges are bound by hand, and the shade is tested on a 2700K bulb before it joins the floor.
